title: What Zen is
hookLine: Chan in China, Seon in Korea, Thien in Vietnam, Zen in Japan: the school of meditation

cards: On a scroll in a meditation hall hangs a single character, brushed in black ink. Show it to a monk in China and she reads it Chan. In Korea, the same brushstrokes are Seon.
In Vietnam, Thien. In Japan, Zen. Four countries, four sounds, one shape on the paper.
In English the word has slipped into a mood: a zen garden, a zen playlist. But on that scroll it names something more particular, a whole school of Buddhism.

teach.b: Chan, Seon, Thien, Zen: these are not four schools that happen to sound alike. They are one Chinese word, carried into neighboring languages and said with each language's own mouth.
Tradition traces the word back to the Sanskrit dhyana, meditation.
So the school's name is, quite plainly, the meditation school. That name puts sitting at the center. For weeks this path has been reading sutras, and Zen communities chant sutras too.
But the name points somewhere else first: not a book on the lap, a body on a cushion, someone who sits down, settles, and looks directly at their own mind.
As the meditation school traveled, each land gave it a voice of its own.

In the coming weeks this path will meet them: Korea's great question, carried through the day; Vietnam's joining of sitting and chanting; in Japan, a school that works with koans and a school of just sitting.
They differ, sometimes, in emphasis. They share the same posture.
So before the poems and the well-known puzzles, before the old masters and the oxherding pictures, comes the body: how to sit, where the hands go, where the eyes rest, what to do with the breath.
That's not a warm-up for Zen. As some Zen teachers put it, it is Zen.

how: Chan, Seon, Thien and Zen communities in China, Korea, Vietnam, Japan and beyond gather to sit in meditation, usually alongside chanting, ritual and work, and many centers welcome beginners to sit with them.

practice: On one out-breath, say quietly, Chan, and let the sound fade; on the next, Seon, then Thien, then Zen, resting in the quiet each one leaves behind. Notice that the names are different and the quiet after them is the same.
Then let the words go and just sit, the way someone has sat in each of those countries.

wordCard.voice: Zen. The Japanese reading of a word that is Chan in China, Seon in Korea and Thien in Vietnam: the meditation school of Buddhism. Today's word.
